title: Common Core SL.CCR.6 Explained
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart closes his walk through the Speaking and Listening anchor standards with SL.CCR.6, which asks students to adapt speech to context and show command of formal English when appropriate. He reads the standard through linguistics rather than through grammar policing: there are many beautiful dialects of English, but one of them is power-laden, and the standard exists because students need access to it. Borrowing Lisa Delpit's phrase, he frames the teacher's job as equipping students with the language of power rather than demeaning the dialect they bring from home. He then routes the standard back through his recurring TAP frame - task, audience, purpose - as the decision tool students themselves can use about how to speak in a given setting. The competence underneath, he argues, is code switching, and he illustrates it against himself: borrowing students' vocabulary to build rapport, and sliding into his Baltimore students' grammatical patterns until their laughter stopped him. Rather than settle the politics of the standard, he ends by handing the hard questions to readers, asking whether a language of power framing is disrespectful and whether Standard American English belongs in every classroom.
points: The central reframe is access rather than correction: teaching Standard American English is presented as equipping students with Delpit's language of power, explicitly not as a judgment on home dialect.
Stuart raises the stakes past test performance, arguing that failing to build a strong grasp of SAE paves the way for a frustrating life in the college and career world.
TAP - task, audience, purpose - is offered as the portable student-facing heuristic behind the standard: generous slang with friends, formality with a prospective employer.

He names code switching as the actual skill being assessed and uses his own unconscious dialect shifts as the worked example, which keeps the standard from sounding like a demand for one correct English.
Instead of resolving the controversy he built into the post, he closes with four open questions to teachers, treating the standard's politics as unsettled rather than settled.
quotes: Are there any linguistics nerds out there? You'll like this one. Although there are lots of beautiful dialects of English, there is a power-laden version of English (sometimes known as Standard American English, or SAE), and SL.CCR.6 reminds us that we need to equip students with this important dialect.

This is not about demeaning a student's home dialect; instead, it's about equipping them with what Lisa Delpit calls “the language of power.” This isn't to say that home dialects aren't cool; it is to say that those in power predominantly use SAE. Because of this, we want our students to have access to SAE so that they can be more agile in the college/career world.

More broadly, this anchor standard goes back to TAP: task, audience, purpose. We want our students to use these three considerations to determine how they should speak. For example, we want them to know that in a conversation with friends they can use generous amounts of slang, but in conversations with prospective employers they should speak more formally (depending on the job).

In linguistics, the ability to switch dialects based on context is called code switching. It's when we either consciously or unconsciously change speech patterns for the sake of achieving communicative purposes.

For example, if I am trying to build rapport with students, I find myself using some of their frequently used words. When I taught in Baltimore, I occasionally even found myself slipping into my students' home dialect grammatical patterns (don't worry, their laughter always snapped me out of it!).
